event: Lindisfarne raid — Norse warriors attack the holy island monastery off the Northumbrian coast. The Viking Age begins.
Ragnar Lodbrok's forces sack Paris. The Franks pay 7,000 pounds of silver in danegeld to make them leave.
The Great Heathen Army invades England. Danish warriors under Ivar the Boneless conquer Northumbria, East Anglia, and Mercia.
Battle of Edington — Alfred of Wessex defeats Guthrum's Danes. England is split: Wessex survives in the south, the Danelaw forms in the north.
Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte — Rollo the Viking is granted Normandy by the Frankish king Charles the Simple in exchange for defending the coast.
Erik Bloodaxe, last Viking king of Jorvik, is killed at Stainmore. Norse political rule in England ends.
Norse sailors reach Iceland. Within a decade permanent settlement begins — farmers and outlaws seeking land the jarls cannot control.
Ingólfr Arnarson founds Reykjavík — the first permanent Norse settlement in Iceland. Others follow, claiming land along the coast.
Erik the Red discovers Greenland after being exiled from Iceland for killing his neighbor. He names it Greenland to attract settlers.
Hedeby grows into the largest trading town in Scandinavia. Merchants from as far as Baghdad trade silver, furs, and slaves at its wharves.
Birka's trade network reaches its peak. Arab silver flows north through the Volga route. Prices for furs and amber are high.
Kaupang's harbor is busy with merchant ships from Denmark, Frisia, and the Baltic. A market town thrives on coastal trade.
Silver supplies from the East begin to dry up as the Abbasid Caliphate weakens. Trade patterns in the Norse world shift westward.
Ansgar, the first Christian missionary to Scandinavia, arrives in Denmark. He builds a small church in Hedeby. Most Danes ignore him.
Harald Bluetooth converts to Christianity and begins forcing baptism on the Danes. The old gods are under threat. Not everyone submits willingly.
Iceland adopts Christianity by law at the Althing. The decision is pragmatic — to avoid civil war. The old ways persist in private.
A harsh winter kills livestock across southern Norway. Families who cannot feed themselves take to the sea — some raid, some trade, some settle.
Sickness sweeps through the crowded quarters of Hedeby. Traders bring disease along with goods from the south.
A blood feud between two families in Kaupang escalates after a killing at the market. The local Thing fails to resolve it. Three men are outlawed.
A volcanic eruption in Iceland buries farmland in ash. Settlers on the eastern coast face starvation. Some abandon their farms.
